method: One agent classified each bill against the policyengine-us 2.2.2 source. A second agent, told to refute the call, checked it, and disagreements were settled by hand. pe_paths are the parameter and variable files in that source a reform would set or read. Each reason states PolicyEngine's side in our own words. A Fiscal Lab assumption counts as a lever only when a reform can impose it through policyengine-us, such as a stated premium rise on the benchmark premium the credit reads (slcsp). In 2.2.2 the benchmark parameter (state_rating_area_cost) and slcsp_age_0 also feed the Medicaid cost index (medicaid_slcsp_cost_index), so a reform must apply the change where the credit reads the benchmark, or hold Medicaid cost at baseline. The test is whether a reform can apply the assumption as Fiscal Lab states it to an amount PolicyEngine computes, as with a uniform percentage on slcsp. The amount also needs a base in 2.2.2's certified default dataset, a Microcosm build, which carries no employer-paid or pre-tax premium amounts, so a stated employer premium rise, which a structural reform could move out of taxable wages, has no base and is not a lever. A take-up response fails it: it means choosing which eligible people or units newly enroll, and 2.2.2's take-up flags (on a person, tax unit or SPM unit) have no rate parameter or enrollment model to choose them, so a run would rest on an assignment PolicyEngine does not make. No PolicyEngine number is recorded.

statuses.not_computed: PolicyEngine's levers carry all (full) or most (partial) of the score. A run could be built; none has been.
statuses.pe_gap: The household model and its default dataset offer no lever for the provisions that carry the score: for none of them (none), or for only a minority (partial).

S_1040.reason: 2.2.2 has no drug prices or Part B, Part D or Medicaid drug spending; the small credit and wage effects ride on an unstated private premium change PolicyEngine cannot derive.

S_1096.reason: PolicyEngine has no drug-level spending, generic entry or Part D plan costs; it carries Part D only as the income-related premium surcharge. Private premiums are inputs that do not respond to drug prices, and Fiscal Lab states no premium change a reform could impose, so neither the federal drug savings nor the premium knock-ons can be produced.

S_1105.reason: PolicyEngine has no Medicare Advantage enrollment, plan payments, risk scores or coding adjustment, and Medicare spending per enrollee is one national per-capita parameter. It computes each enrollee's Part B premium from the standard premium plus the income-related adjustment, less Medicare Savings Program coverage, but the standard Part B premium is a set parameter that does not follow Part B spending, so the premium offset and the dual-eligible premium effect cannot be computed.

S_2665.reason: PolicyEngine has no drug supply or FDA reporting representation; the bill changes no tax or benefit rule the model carries.

S_4886.reason: The QMB income limit and the Medicare Savings Program asset test are parameters, so the new Medicare Savings Program premium and cost-sharing payments, a minority of the score, could run. PolicyEngine values QMB cost sharing as a flat share of average Medicare spending and has no take-up step for these programs, so a run would count every newly eligible person, except that the federal cost (msp_federal_cost) leaves out anyone enrolled in full Medicaid. 2.2.2 has no Medicare cost sharing by beneficiary, so the out-of-pocket cap cannot run, and it has no Medicare Advantage or Part D low-income subsidy.
